title: The barrage at El Alamein
body:
At 9:40 p.m. the desert lit up like day.

23 October 1942. Nearly 900 British and Commonwealth guns opened fire at once along the line at El Alamein in Egypt. It was the start of Operation Lightfoot, and the noise rolled across the sand for miles.

Behind the barrage, Montgomery's Eighth Army began clearing paths through the minefields the Germans called the Devil's Gardens.

The timing was cruel for the other side. Rommel was in Germany on sick leave. His stand in, General Georg Stumme, died of a heart attack the next day while driving to the front. Rommel flew back to a battle already underway.

Twelve days later, on 4 November, he ordered the retreat. Back in London, Churchill told the country it was perhaps "the end of the beginning."
photoNote: A 25 pounder gun firing during the night barrage that opened the Second Battle of El Alamein, 23 October 1942. No. 1 Army Film and Photographic Unit, IWM E 18469, public domain (Crown copyright expired).

threads:
At 9:40 p.m. the desert lit up like day.

23 October 1942. Nearly 900 British and Commonwealth guns fired at once at El Alamein in Egypt, opening Montgomery's great offensive.

Rommel was home in Germany on sick leave. His stand in died of a heart attack the next day. Twelve days later, the Afrika Korps was in retreat.

video.note: Desert Victory (1943), British Ministry of Information documentary with film shot by the Army Film and Photographic Unit; Crown copyright expired, public domain (PD-UKGov on Wikimedia Commons; Commons 480p copy). The night gun flashes of the 23 Oct 1942 barrage are genuine footage (the staged Pinewood close ups of soldiers are not used). Clip uses 29:21.27 to 29:24.0, then 27:07.36 to 27:20.2. Sound: the film's own soundtrack under these shots (gunfire, no music or narration), mixed for the 1943 film, cut with the picture and loudness normalized.

kit.filmCaption: Film from El Alamein, 23 October 1942. At 9:40 p.m. nearly 900 British and Commonwealth guns opened fire, and army cameramen filmed the flashes in the dark. From the 1943 British documentary Desert Victory.
